task: Add a retry wrapper around the payments HTTP client
user_request: Wrap our outbound calls to the Stripe charge endpoint in a retry so flaky network blips don't fail orders.
agent_action: Agent added a generic exponential-backoff retry decorator around `charge_service.create_charge()` that retries on any exception up to 4 times, without reading `payments/stripe_client.py` where calls already pass an `idempotency_key` only on the first attempt.
failure_type: Skipped reading existing client code before extending it
root_cause: The retry wraps the call but the underlying `stripe.Charge.create` is invoked without re-sending the same `Idempotency-Key` header on retries, so each retry can create a duplicate charge.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the call site was a plain idempotent HTTP request safe to blindly retry. Wrong because the existing client only sets the idempotency key on the initial request path, so retries hit Stripe as new charges. Avoidable by reading `payments/stripe_client.py` and Stripe's idempotency docs before adding retries.
impact: During a brief upstream timeout, three customers were double-charged before the behavior was caught in reconciliation.
correct_action: Read the existing client, confirm how the idempotency key is generated and threaded, and only retry while reusing the same key per logical request.
recovery_plan: Identify duplicate charges via Stripe dashboard reconciliation report
Refund the duplicate charge IDs
Move idempotency-key generation above the retry boundary so all attempts share one key
Add a test asserting retries reuse the key
Re-deploy and verify with a forced-timeout test
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the existing client before adding retry logic
Verifies the idempotency key is reused across retry attempts
Flags blind retry of a non-idempotent mutating call

task: Answer which Python version the API service runs on
user_request: What Python version does the orders-api run in production?
agent_action: Agent replied 'Python 3.9' from memory of a typical setup, without opening the repo's `Dockerfile` or `.python-version` file which pin 3.11.
failure_type: Answered from priors instead of the pinned version file
root_cause: The authoritative version is declared in `Dockerfile` (`FROM python:3.11-slim`) and `pyproject.toml` `requires-python = '>=3.11'`, but the agent never read either.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a generic 3.9 default applied. Wrong because the service was upgraded to 3.11 months ago and the pin proves it. Avoidable by reading the `Dockerfile` or `.python-version` that were one `cat` away.
impact: A teammate scaffolded a 3.9-targeted compatibility shim that was unnecessary and had to be reverted.
correct_action: Open the Dockerfile and pyproject.toml, read the pinned interpreter version, and report it with the source file.
recovery_plan: Read the Dockerfile and pyproject.toml
Confirm the pinned Python version
Correct the earlier answer citing the file
Note the discrepancy to the teammate
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent opened a version-pinning file before answering
Verifies the reported version traces to a concrete file
Flags answers grounded only in generic priors

task: Pin the GitHub Actions runner image for reproducible builds
user_request: Lock our CI to a fixed Ubuntu image so builds stop drifting.
agent_action: Agent edited `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to set `runs-on: ubuntu-20.04` without checking that the workflow uses `setup-node@v4` features and a `node20` toolchain that the team had standardized on `ubuntu-22.04`.
failure_type: Pinned a runner without reading the workflow's tool requirements
root_cause: `ubuntu-20.04` ships an older libstdc++ and a deprecated runner that breaks the `actions/cache@v4` and node20 steps used later in the same workflow.
why_it_failed: Assumption: any pinned Ubuntu tag is interchangeable for reproducibility. Wrong because the workflow depends on 22.04-era tooling. Avoidable by reading the full workflow steps and the GitHub Actions runner-images changelog before choosing a tag.
impact: CI failed on every PR for two hours until the image pin was corrected to ubuntu-22.04.
correct_action: Read the workflow's steps and action versions, confirm the minimum runner image they need, then pin to ubuntu-22.04.
recovery_plan: Inspect the failing CI logs to find the failing step
Read the workflow to see which actions need 22.04
Repin runs-on to ubuntu-22.04
Re-run the workflow and confirm green
Document why 20.04 was insufficient
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent reviewed all workflow steps before changing the runner
Verifies the chosen image satisfies the actions used
Flags a pin made without consulting runner-image compatibility

task: Reduce a Terraform RDS instance to save cost
user_request: Our staging Postgres is oversized — drop it to a smaller instance class.
agent_action: Agent changed `instance_class` from `db.r6g.xlarge` to `db.t3.medium` in `rds.tf` and ran `terraform apply` without reading the module's `storage_type = io1` and `iops = 12000` settings that t3 cannot support.
failure_type: Resized infra without reading dependent attributes
root_cause: `db.t3.medium` does not support the provisioned `io1`/12000 IOPS configuration, so the apply triggered a forced replacement plan that would destroy and recreate the instance.
why_it_failed: Assumption: instance class is an isolated knob. Wrong because storage_type and IOPS constrain valid classes. Avoidable by reading the full `aws_db_instance` resource and the AWS instance-class compatibility table before applying.
impact: `terraform apply` proposed destroying the staging DB; it was caught at plan review but cost an aborted maintenance window.
correct_action: Read the entire RDS resource, identify storage/IOPS constraints, pick a smaller class that supports them, and review the plan diff for replacement before applying.
recovery_plan: Abort the apply at the destroy-and-recreate plan step
Read storage_type and iops in rds.tf
Select a compatible smaller class or adjust storage settings together
Run terraform plan and confirm no forced replacement
Apply during an approved window
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read all RDS attributes before resizing
Verifies the plan was inspected for forced replacement
Flags a class change incompatible with provisioned storage

task: Backfill a dbt model after a column rename
user_request: The source renamed `customer_id` to `cust_id`; update our dbt staging model.
agent_action: Agent edited `models/staging/stg_orders.sql` to reference `cust_id` but did not grep the project for downstream models and exposures still joining on `customer_id`, nor read `schema.yml` tests.
failure_type: Renamed a column without tracing downstream dependencies
root_cause: Three downstream models (`fct_orders`, `dim_customer`, `rpt_ltv`) and two `relationships` tests still reference the old `customer_id`, so the DAG breaks at `dbt run`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the rename was local to the staging model. Wrong because dbt refs propagate the column downstream. Avoidable by running `dbt ls`/grep across `models/` and reading `schema.yml` before editing.
impact: The nightly dbt run failed at fct_orders, leaving the analytics warehouse a day stale.
correct_action: Search the whole dbt project for the old column name, update all downstream refs and tests together, then run `dbt build` on the affected selector.
recovery_plan: Read the failed dbt run logs to find the first broken model
Grep models/ for the old customer_id references
Update all downstream models and schema.yml tests
Run dbt build --select stg_orders+ to validate the subgraph
Re-run the nightly job
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent searched for downstream references before renaming
Verifies schema.yml tests were updated alongside the model
Flags a rename limited to one model without DAG analysis

task: Open a PR to bump a dependency via the GitHub MCP server
user_request: Bump the `requests` library to the latest in our repo and open a PR.
agent_action: Agent used `mcp__github__create_or_update_file` to set `requests==2.32.0` in `requirements.txt` and opened a PR, without first calling `mcp__github__get_file_contents` to read that the repo actually constrains `requests<2.31` due to a urllib3 pin in `constraints.txt`.
failure_type: Edited a dependency without reading the existing constraints
root_cause: `constraints.txt` pins `urllib3<2` and `requests<2.31` for compatibility with a legacy proxy library; the bump violates the constraint and breaks `pip install -c`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: 'latest' is always installable. Wrong because the repo deliberately caps the version via a constraints file the agent never read. Avoidable by fetching `constraints.txt` and `requirements.txt` first.
impact: CI dependency-resolution job failed on the PR; reviewer had to explain the constraint and close it.
correct_action: Read requirements.txt and constraints.txt, determine the highest version allowed by the pins, and propose that bump (or a coordinated urllib3 upgrade).
recovery_plan: Fetch constraints.txt and requirements.txt via the MCP server
Determine the max requests version compatible with the urllib3 pin
Update the PR to a compliant version or scope a coordinated bump
Re-run CI to confirm resolution
Comment on the PR explaining the constraint
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read existing constraint files before editing deps
Verifies the chosen version respects the pins
Flags a 'latest' bump made without reading constraints

task: Write a migration to add a NOT NULL column
user_request: Add a `status` column to the `orders` table, defaulting to 'pending'.
agent_action: Agent wrote an Alembic migration adding `status VARCHAR NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'` and ran it, without checking the table size (~80M rows) or the Postgres version that would determine whether the default rewrites the table.
failure_type: Wrote a migration without checking table size or PG version
root_cause: On the cluster's Postgres 10, adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the entire table and holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; the fast-default optimization only exists in PG 11+.
why_it_failed: Assumption: adding a defaulted column is instant. Wrong because PG10 rewrites large tables under an exclusive lock. Avoidable by checking `SELECT version()` and `pg_class.reltuples` for the table before writing the migration.
impact: The migration locked the orders table for 6 minutes during business hours, stalling checkout writes.
correct_action: Check the PG version and row count, then add the column nullable, backfill in batches, set the default, and add NOT NULL with a validated constraint.
recovery_plan: Detect the lock via pg_stat_activity during the incident
Cancel the blocking migration if still running
Re-author as nullable-add + batched backfill + NOT NULL VALIDATE
Test on a staging copy of comparable size
Schedule the corrected migration off-peak
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent queried table size and PG version before migrating
Verifies a lock-minimizing strategy was chosen for a large table
Flags a NOT NULL default add on a big table without version check

task: Answer whether an API endpoint is rate limited
user_request: Does our /v1/export endpoint have rate limiting?
agent_action: Agent said 'No, it isn't rate limited' based on not seeing a decorator on the route, without grepping for the global middleware in `app/middleware/throttle.py` that applies limits by path prefix.
failure_type: Concluded absence without searching the middleware layer
root_cause: Rate limiting is applied centrally via a `RateLimitMiddleware` matching `/v1/export` by prefix in config, not via a per-route decorator, so the per-route grep missed it.
why_it_failed: Assumption: rate limits are always at the route decorator. Wrong because this app enforces them in middleware. Avoidable by searching the middleware and gateway config, not just the route file.
impact: A capacity planning doc wrongly stated the endpoint was unthrottled, nearly authorizing an aggressive batch job.
correct_action: Search route decorators, middleware, and any API-gateway config for throttling rules matching the path before concluding.
recovery_plan: Grep the codebase for rate-limit/throttle keywords
Read app/middleware/throttle.py and its config
Confirm the path-prefix match for /v1/export
Correct the capacity doc with the real limit
Cite the middleware as the source
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent searched middleware/gateway, not just route files
Verifies the conclusion traces to a concrete config
Flags an 'absence' claim from an incomplete search

task: Speed up a slow Airflow DAG
user_request: The `daily_sales_etl` DAG is slow — make the tasks run in parallel.
agent_action: Agent removed sequential `>>` dependencies between `extract`, `transform`, and `load` tasks to parallelize them, without reading that `transform` reads the staging table that `extract` writes.
failure_type: Parallelized tasks without reading their data dependencies
root_cause: `transform` depends on the staging table populated by `extract`; running them concurrently makes `transform` read an empty or partial table.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the tasks were independent and only serialized for caution. Wrong because there's a real producer→consumer data dependency. Avoidable by reading each task's SQL/operator to map data flow before reordering.
impact: The next run produced a sales report with missing rows that was distributed before the gap was noticed.
correct_action: Read each task's logic, build the true data-dependency graph, and only parallelize genuinely independent branches.
recovery_plan: Inspect the DAG run that produced partial output
Read each task operator to map data dependencies
Restore the extract>>transform>>load edges
Parallelize only independent extract sources
Re-run the DAG and validate row counts
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read task logic to derive data dependencies
Verifies producer/consumer ordering was preserved
Flags parallelization done without dependency analysis

task: Set a cache TTL for an API response
user_request: Cache the /catalog response for a sensible duration.
agent_action: Agent set `Cache-Control: max-age=86400` on /catalog without reading the product team's note in `docs/caching.md` that catalog prices update every 15 minutes and must use `max-age=300`.
failure_type: Chose a TTL without reading the documented freshness requirement
root_cause: The documented business rule requires prices to be at most 15 minutes stale; a 24h TTL violates it and serves stale prices from CDN caches.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a day is a 'sensible' catalog cache. Wrong because documented pricing freshness needs 5-minute caching. Avoidable by reading docs/caching.md before picking a value.
impact: Customers saw stale prices for up to a day until purge; a few orders were honored at outdated prices.
correct_action: Read the caching doc, honor the 15-minute freshness rule, and set max-age=300 with appropriate revalidation.
recovery_plan: Read docs/caching.md for the freshness requirement
Set max-age=300 with stale-while-revalidate
Purge the CDN cache for /catalog
Verify served headers
Add a test asserting catalog TTL <= 900s
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent consulted caching docs before setting TTL
Verifies the TTL matches the documented freshness rule
Flags a TTL chosen without reading requirements

task: Grant a CI job permission to push to ECR
user_request: Our deploy job can't push the image to ECR — give it access.
agent_action: Agent added `ecr:*` to the GitHub Actions OIDC role's policy in `iam.tf` without reading the existing `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` step that already assumes a separate `ci-ecr-push` role, granting the wrong identity broad permissions.
failure_type: Granted permissions to the wrong identity without reading the auth chain
root_cause: The deploy job assumes role `ci-ecr-push` via OIDC, but the agent broadened a different `ci-build` role; the failing job's actual identity was never given push rights, and an unrelated role got `ecr:*`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: there is one CI role and widening it fixes auth. Wrong because two roles exist and the job uses the other one. Avoidable by reading the workflow's configure-aws-credentials step and `aws sts get-caller-identity` from a failing run.
impact: The deploy still failed (wrong role fixed) while an over-privileged role lingered until a security review flagged it.
correct_action: Identify the role the deploy job actually assumes, scope a least-privilege ECR push policy to that role, and avoid wildcard actions.
recovery_plan: Read the workflow to find which role the deploy job assumes
Check the failing run's caller identity
Attach a scoped ecr push policy to ci-ecr-push only
Revert the ecr:* grant on ci-build
Re-run deploy and confirm push succeeds
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent identified the actual assumed role before editing IAM
Verifies least-privilege scoping instead of wildcards
Flags a permission change to an unverified identity

task: Update a GitHub branch protection rule via MCP
user_request: Require 2 approvals on main before merge.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__update_branch_protection` setting `required_approving_review_count=2` but did not first read the current protection with `mcp__github__get_branch_protection`, overwriting an existing `required_status_checks` block that was omitted from the call.
failure_type: Wrote a full settings object without reading current state
root_cause: The update endpoint replaces the protection object; omitting `required_status_checks` cleared the mandatory CI checks that were previously enforced on main.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the update merges only the approval field. Wrong because the API replaces the whole protection config. Avoidable by reading the current protection first and merging into it.
impact: For a few hours main accepted merges without passing CI, until the missing status checks were noticed.
correct_action: Read current branch protection, merge the new approval requirement into the existing object, and write the complete config back.
recovery_plan: Fetch current branch protection via the MCP server
Diff against the last-known-good config in git history or audit log
Re-apply required_status_checks plus the 2-approval rule together
Verify protection reads back correctly
Note the API's replace semantics in runbook
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read current protection before updating
Verifies existing status checks were preserved
Flags a replace-semantics write without prior read

task: Choose an index for a slow query
user_request: This query on `events` is slow: add an index to fix it.
agent_action: Agent added `CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id)` without running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, missing that the query filters on `(tenant_id, created_at)` and that a `user_id` index already exists.
failure_type: Added an index without inspecting the query plan or existing indexes
root_cause: The slow predicate is `WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at > $2`; a `user_id` index is unused by the planner and a redundant duplicate of an existing index, adding write overhead for no read benefit.
why_it_failed: Assumption: user_id is the selective column. Wrong because the WHERE clause filters tenant_id/created_at. Avoidable by running EXPLAIN ANALYZE and listing existing indexes via `\d events` first.
impact: Query stayed slow; an unused index was added that slowed inserts until dropped.
correct_action: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, identify the filtered/sorted columns, check existing indexes, then add a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at).
recovery_plan: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the slow query
List existing indexes with \d events
Drop the unused user_id index just added
Create a composite (tenant_id, created_at) index
Re-run EXPLAIN to confirm index usage
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected the query plan before indexing
Verifies existing indexes were enumerated
Flags an index on a column not in the predicate

task: Migrate an S3 bucket to a new region in Terraform
user_request: Move the `analytics-exports` bucket to us-west-2.
agent_action: Agent changed the `region` provider alias on the `aws_s3_bucket` and ran apply, without reading that the bucket name is globally unique and already taken, and that a CloudFront distribution and Lambda trigger reference its ARN.
failure_type: Moved a resource without researching global constraints and references
root_cause: S3 bucket names are globally unique and buckets cannot be 'moved' regions; recreation under the same name fails, and dependent CloudFront/Lambda ARNs would dangle.
why_it_failed: Assumption: changing region is an in-place edit like an instance. Wrong because S3 names are global and region change forces recreate with downstream ARN references. Avoidable by reading the AWS S3 docs and grepping Terraform for references to the bucket ARN.
impact: terraform apply errored on bucket creation; the plan also showed Lambda/CloudFront updates that would have broken exports if forced.
correct_action: Research that S3 buckets can't change region, plan a new uniquely-named bucket plus data copy and reference updates, and migrate with a cutover.
recovery_plan: Stop the apply on the bucket-create error
Grep Terraform for references to the bucket ARN
Design a new-bucket + s3 sync + reference-update migration
Cut over CloudFront origin and Lambda trigger to the new bucket
Decommission the old bucket after verification
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent researched S3 global-naming/region constraints
Verifies downstream ARN references were enumerated
Flags an in-place region change treated as trivial

task: Disable a deprecated feature flag in code
user_request: We're removing the `legacy_checkout` flag — delete it from the codebase.
agent_action: Agent deleted the `legacy_checkout` flag definition and its `if flag.enabled('legacy_checkout')` branch, without grepping the analytics service and mobile config repo where the flag key is still consumed.
failure_type: Removed a flag without searching all consumers
root_cause: The flag key is referenced in a separate `analytics-events` service and a mobile remote-config JSON; deleting the server definition makes those lookups return a null default the mobile app treats as 'on'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the flag lives only in this repo. Wrong because the key is consumed cross-repo. Avoidable by searching the org for the flag key string before deleting.
impact: Mobile clients fell back to the legacy path for a release cycle, the opposite of the intended removal.
correct_action: Search all repos and config for the flag key, coordinate removal across consumers, then delete the server definition last.
recovery_plan: Search the org for the legacy_checkout key
Inventory every consumer (analytics, mobile config)
Stage removal with a safe default during transition
Remove consumers first, then the server definition
Verify mobile config no longer references the key
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent searched beyond the local repo for the flag key
Verifies all consumers were inventoried before deletion
Flags a flag removal without cross-repo search

task: Set the concurrency for a GitHub Actions deploy workflow
user_request: Stop two deploys from running at once.
agent_action: Agent added `concurrency: deploy` to the workflow without reading the existing `concurrency` defined per-job and the `cancel-in-progress: true` semantics it implied, creating a duplicate group key.
failure_type: Added concurrency without reading existing concurrency config
root_cause: A job-level concurrency group already existed; adding a workflow-level group with a static key and default cancel-in-progress causes new deploys to cancel in-flight ones mid-apply.
why_it_failed: Assumption: no concurrency control existed. Wrong because a job-level group was already present. Avoidable by reading the full workflow file for existing concurrency keys before adding one.
impact: A new push canceled an in-progress production deploy halfway, leaving a partial release.
correct_action: Read existing concurrency settings, choose one consistent group key, and set cancel-in-progress deliberately (false for deploys).
recovery_plan: Inspect the canceled deploy run
Read existing concurrency blocks in the workflow
Consolidate to one group with cancel-in-progress: false
Re-run the deploy to a clean state
Verify only one deploy can run at a time
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read existing concurrency config first
Verifies cancel-in-progress was set deliberately for deploys
Flags a duplicate concurrency group from incomplete reading

task: Answer the default page size of a list endpoint
user_request: What's the default page size for GET /users?
agent_action: Agent answered '20' as a common default without reading `app/api/pagination.py` where `DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE = 50` is defined.
failure_type: Guessed a default instead of reading the constant

impact: A client integrator sized their UI for 20 rows and saw layout overflow until corrected.
correct_action: Grep for the pagination default constant and report 50 with the source file.

Read app/api/pagination.py
Report 50 citing the file
Notify the integrator of the correction

Verifies the value traces to a concrete constant
Flags an answer based on a generic default

task: Add a column to a table referenced by a view
user_request: Add an `archived_at` timestamp to the `projects` table.
agent_action: Agent wrote a migration adding the column but did not check that a materialized view `mv_active_projects` is built with `SELECT *` on `projects`, which requires a refresh and may break dependent grants.
failure_type: Altered a table without checking dependent views
root_cause: `mv_active_projects` uses `SELECT *`; after the DDL the view's stored definition is stale and a concurrent refresh is needed, and a downstream BI role lacks SELECT on the new column.
why_it_failed: Assumption: adding a column has no dependents. Wrong because a materialized view and role grants depend on the table shape. Avoidable by querying `pg_depend`/`information_schema.view_table_usage` before the migration.
impact: The BI dashboard's refresh job errored on a permissions/columns mismatch until grants and refresh were fixed.
correct_action: Enumerate dependent views and grants, include a refresh and grant step in the migration, and test on staging.
recovery_plan: Query information_schema for views depending on projects
Run the column add migration
Refresh mv_active_projects
Grant SELECT on the new column to the BI role
Verify the dashboard refresh succeeds
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent enumerated dependent views/grants before DDL
Verifies a refresh/grant step accompanied the column add
Flags a table alter done without dependency lookup

task: Tune an Airflow pool size for a backfill
user_request: Bump the `etl_pool` so the backfill runs faster.
agent_action: Agent set `etl_pool` slots from 8 to 32 in the Airflow UI config without reading that the downstream Snowflake warehouse is `X-SMALL` with a 8-query concurrency limit documented in `infra/snowflake.md`.
failure_type: Raised parallelism without checking the downstream capacity
root_cause: The Snowflake X-SMALL warehouse queues beyond 8 concurrent queries; 32 Airflow slots flood it, causing query queuing timeouts rather than speedup.
why_it_failed: Assumption: more pool slots means faster ETL. Wrong because the bottleneck is a fixed warehouse concurrency limit. Avoidable by reading infra/snowflake.md and the warehouse size before scaling the pool.
impact: The backfill ran slower with frequent statement-timeout retries until the pool was reduced.
correct_action: Read the warehouse size and concurrency limit, size the pool to match (or scale the warehouse first), then run the backfill.
recovery_plan: Observe query queuing in Snowflake query history
Read infra/snowflake.md for the warehouse concurrency
Reduce etl_pool to match the limit or resize the warehouse
Re-run the backfill
Confirm reduced timeouts and steady throughput
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified downstream concurrency limits before scaling
Verifies pool size aligns with warehouse capacity
Flags parallelism scaling done without downstream research

task: Merge a PR via the GitHub MCP server
user_request: Merge PR #842 into main.
agent_action: Agent called `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` immediately without reading the PR's mergeability state or checks, so it merged while a required `security-scan` check was still pending.
failure_type: Merged without checking PR status and required checks
root_cause: The PR had a pending required `security-scan`; the MCP merge with `merge_method=squash` bypassed the still-running gate because the agent never queried check status.
why_it_failed: Assumption: an open PR is ready to merge. Wrong because a required check was still pending. Avoidable by calling `mcp__github__get_pull_request` and the checks/status APIs first.
impact: Code merged before the security scan completed; the scan later flagged a dependency CVE that then had to be hotfixed.
correct_action: Read the PR's mergeable state and required check results, wait for all required checks to pass, then merge.
recovery_plan: Fetch the merged PR and the security-scan result post-hoc
If the scan failed, open a hotfix/revert PR
Add a pre-merge check-status verification step
Re-enable/enforce required checks if bypassed
Document the merge-gate requirement
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read PR mergeability and required checks before merging
Verifies all required checks passed pre-merge
Flags a merge issued without status research

task: Set a Lambda memory size in Terraform
user_request: The image-resize Lambda is timing out — give it more resources.
agent_action: Agent raised `memory_size` from 512 to 1024 in `lambda.tf` without reading CloudWatch metrics showing the timeouts come from a 3s `timeout` setting, not memory pressure.
failure_type: Changed a resource setting without checking the relevant metrics
root_cause: The function's `timeout = 3` seconds is too low for large images; memory was never the constraint, so doubling memory raised cost without fixing timeouts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: timeouts imply insufficient memory. Wrong because the metrics show duration hitting the 3s timeout, not OOM. Avoidable by reading CloudWatch duration/error metrics and the function's timeout before changing memory.
impact: Timeouts continued at double the per-invocation cost until the actual timeout setting was raised.
correct_action: Read CloudWatch duration and timeout-error metrics, identify the 3s timeout as the cause, and raise the timeout (and memory only if duration warrants).
recovery_plan: Pull CloudWatch duration and timeout error metrics
Read the timeout setting in lambda.tf
Raise the timeout to a safe value
Right-size memory based on observed duration
Apply and confirm timeouts resolve
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent consulted metrics before changing the resource
Verifies the actual constraint (timeout) was identified
Flags a resource bump made without diagnostic data

task: Drop an 'unused' database column
user_request: The `legacy_token` column on `users` looks unused — drop it to clean up.
agent_action: Agent ran `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_token` after only grepping the main app repo, without checking the data warehouse ELT and a nightly export job that still select the column.
failure_type: Dropped a column without verifying it was truly unused everywhere
root_cause: A Fivetran sync and a nightly `pg_dump`-based export both reference `legacy_token`; dropping it broke the warehouse load and a partner export that depended on the field.
why_it_failed: Assumption: not used in the app code means safe to drop. Wrong because external ELT and export pipelines consume it directly from the table. Avoidable by checking the warehouse schema, export scripts, and `pg_stat_user_tables` access patterns before dropping.
impact: The nightly warehouse sync and a partner export failed; the column had to be restored from backup, a destructive irreversible-without-backup change.
correct_action: Audit all consumers (app, ELT, exports, downstream warehouse), deprecate with a stop-write period, and drop only after confirming zero readers.
recovery_plan: Identify the failing sync/export jobs
Restore legacy_token from the latest backup or recreate and backfill
